title: Mindfulness in schools
hook: a large UK trial found school mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching (Kuyken et al., 2022)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mindfulness without ethics, and the question of what calm is for. Your line was not just calm. What job did you give yours? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

Third period, a classroom of teenagers. The teacher dims the lights and asks everyone to close their eyes and notice the breath. A few actually do. One stares at the ceiling tiles. A couple in the back are trying hard not to laugh. Somebody's phone buzzes in a backpack. It's a lovely idea on paper: teach every child, early, the skills adults pay for later. So researchers in the United Kingdom set out to test it properly, across a great many schools, over years. The answer they got was not the one its supporters hoped for. Today is that answer, and what it says about invitation.
screen: `EYES CLOSED, THIRD PERIOD.` → `A LOVELY IDEA ON PAPER.` → `TESTED PROPERLY.`

segments.voice: First, the trial. A team led by Willem Kuyken ran a large study in UK secondary schools. Some schools, chosen at random, taught a mindfulness course with trained teachers. Others kept their usual lessons on social and emotional health. Then the researchers followed the students over time. Second, the result. The mindfulness lessons did no better than the usual teaching for students' mental health. Not worse. Not better. The researchers also reported that a lot of students did little of the practice outside class. Third, what that does and doesn't mean. It doesn't show that mindfulness harms young people, or that it does nothing for adults who choose it. It shows something narrower: a practice handed to a whole class, required, on a timetable, didn't do what was hoped. One reading: choosing may matter. Fourth, an old picture of invitation. In the book of Revelation, in the King James text, Jesus speaks to a church this way: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him." In that picture, even the one knocking doesn't break the door down. He knocks, and waits, and the door opens from the inside. Some readers hear a whole approach to practice in that picture. A practice offered can be taken up. A practice imposed tends to get endured.
screen: `SCHOOLS CHOSEN AT RANDOM.` · `NO BETTER, NO WORSE.` · `CHOOSING MAY MATTER.` · `I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.` · then, large: `INVITE, DON'T FORCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the door, don't push it. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person you've wished would try practice, or prayer, or quiet. A child, a partner, a friend, a parent. Notice any pushing in you, the wanting them to. Breathe with that for a moment. Then let it soften into something simpler: wishing them well, whether they ever sit or not. If you pray, you can hold them that way in prayer. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mindfulness in schools. A large UK trial found mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching, a reminder that a practice can be offered but not imposed. Today's word.
Your line: invite, don't force. Today, if your practice comes up, mention it once, lightly, and leave the door open. Then let it go. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some schools offer mindfulness lessons as part of their teaching; teachers of contemplative practice often stress that it works best when people choose it rather than being made to do it.

trapdoor: what you thought: if mindfulness is good, every child should be taught it in school.
what it means: a large UK trial found the lessons did no better than usual teaching. one reading: choosing may matter.
what a scholar hears: Kuyken's trial randomized schools, compared mindfulness with usual social-emotional teaching, and noted low home practice.

sources.ref: Kuyken et al., MYRIAD trial, "Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of universal school-based mindfulness training compared with normal school provision" (Evidence-Based Mental Health)

notes: Confirm the MYRIAD summary: cluster-randomized trial in UK secondary schools; schools allocated to school-based mindfulness training (taught by trained schoolteachers) or usual social-emotional learning; no evidence of superiority on mental health outcomes; follow-up over time. Numbers of schools and students deliberately left out ('a great many schools', 'over years').
Confirm that the MYRIAD papers report low student engagement and little home practice; the voice says 'a lot of students did little of the practice outside class'.
Revelation 3:20 is cited as a Christian picture of invitation; check that the gloss ('even the one knocking doesn't break the door down') is fair and not a doctrinal claim.
'Some readers hear a whole approach to practice in that picture' is attributed to some readers, not stated as a tradition's teaching.
The classroom scene in the hook is illustrative.
Editor pass: 'choosing seems to matter' (voice, screen, trapdoor) became 'one reading: choosing may matter', since the trial compared required courses with usual teaching and did not test choice.
